test.explanation: A maximum of five members may be hoisted per lift, and only beams and similar structural members may be lifted (1926.753(e)(1)(ii)-(iii)). Job-site scenario: a christmas-tree lift of five beams is the limit.

test.question: Under 1926.754(e)(5)(i), when must metal decking be secured (outside a controlled decking zone)?
options: Laid tightly and immediately secured upon placement
At the end of the shift
At the end of the week
test.explanation: Except in a controlled decking zone under 1926.760(c), metal decking must be laid tightly and immediately secured upon placement (1926.754(e)(5)(i)). Bundles must also be secured at the end of the shift or when conditions require (1926.754(e)(1)(v)). Job-site scenario: each sheet is tack-welded or screwed as it is placed.

test.question: During steel erection, how may a crane hoist employees under 1926.753(c)(4)?
options: On the hook or headache ball
On a personnel platform, provided all provisions of 1926.1431 (except 1926.1431(a)) are met
test.explanation: Cranes or derricks may hoist employees on a personnel platform during steel erection, provided all provisions of 1926.1431 except 1926.1431(a) are met (1926.753(c)(4)). Job-site scenario: bolt-up crews ride a certified personnel platform rigged per 1926.1431, never the hook.

test.question: Under 1926.753(d)(1), which employees may work directly below a suspended load during steel erection?
options: Only employees engaged in the initial connection of the steel, or those needed to hook or unhook the load
Anyone if the load is under 1 ton
test.explanation: Routes for suspended loads must be pre-planned so no employee works directly below a suspended load, except employees engaged in the initial connection of the steel or those needed to hook or unhook the load (1926.753(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the decking crew moves aside while the beam swings over.

test.question: Under 1926.761(a), who must provide the training required by the steel erection standard?
test.explanation: Training required by 1926.761 must be provided by a qualified person (1926.761(a)). Each employee exposed to a fall hazard must be trained in recognizing hazards and using fall protection systems (1926.761(b)). Job-site scenario: a qualified trainer delivers the connector and decking training before the raising gang starts.

title: Electrical Safety Fundamentals
topics: GFCI or assured equipment grounding program

resources.title: Ground Fault Protection
resources.description: GFCI and assured equipment grounding conductor program requirements

resources.title: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
resources.description: Protection of employees from energized circuits

test.question: Under 1926.404(b)(1)(ii), which receptacles need GFCI protection if the employer uses the GFCI option?
options: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles on construction sites that are not part of the building's permanent wiring and are in use by employees
test.explanation: The employer must use either GFCIs or an assured equipment grounding conductor program (1926.404(b)(1)(i)). Under the GFCI option, all 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles not part of the permanent wiring and in use by employees need GFCIs. Small listed generators are exempt (1926.404(b)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: every temporary-power outlet on the spider box is GFCI-protected.

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(1), when may an employee work close enough to contact part of an electric power circuit?
options: Whenever they stay at least 1 foot away
Only when protected against electric shock by deenergizing and grounding the circuit, or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means
test.explanation: No employee may work in proximity to any part of an electric power circuit they could contact unless protected by deenergizing and grounding the circuit or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means (1926.416(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: before pulling wire near a live bus, the circuit is deenergized and grounded, or the bus is covered with insulating blankets.

test.question: Under an assured equipment grounding conductor program, when must the required tests be performed (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E))?
options: Before first use, after repairs, after any incident suspected of causing damage, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months (6 months for fixed cord sets and receptacles not exposed to damage)
test.explanation: Tests are required before first use, before return to service after repairs, before use after a suspected-damage incident, and at least every 3 months (6 months for fixed cord sets and receptacles not exposed to damage) (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E)). Cords and equipment must also be visually inspected before each day's use (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(C)), and tests must be recorded (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(G)). Job-site scenario: a cord run over by a skid steer is retested before reuse.

test.question: What does 1926.404(a)(1) require of an equipment grounding conductor?
options: It must be the largest conductor
It must be identifiable and distinguishable from all other conductors
test.explanation: A conductor used as an equipment grounding conductor must be identifiable and distinguishable from all other conductors (1926.404(a)(1)). Green (or bare) is the common electrical-code convention, but that color is not stated in 1926 text. Job-site scenario: the electrician confirms the cord's grounding conductor goes to the grounding terminal and polarity is not reversed (1926.404(a)(2)).

test.question: Under 1926.416(d), what must be used when fuses are installed or removed with one or both terminals energized?
options: Special tools insulated for the voltage
Pliers with tape on the handles
test.explanation: When fuses are installed or removed with one or both terminals energized, special tools insulated for the voltage must be used (1926.416(d)). Job-site scenario: the electrician uses a rated fuse puller on the live disconnect.

test.question: What does 1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(E) require for temporary lighting?
options: Lamps for general illumination must be protected from accidental contact or breakage, and metal-case sockets must be grounded
test.explanation: All lamps for general illumination must be protected from accidental contact or breakage, and metal-case sockets must be grounded (1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(E)). Job-site scenario: temporary string lights in the stairwell have cage guards on every bulb.

test.question: How must flexible cords be protected on a job site?
options: They must be protected from damage, and extension cords may not be fastened with staples, hung from nails, or suspended by wire
test.explanation: Flexible cords and cables must be protected from damage, avoiding sharp corners and projections (1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(I)). Extension cords may not be stapled, hung from nails, or suspended by wire (1926.416(e)(2)), and worn or frayed cords may not be used (1926.416(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: cords crossing a doorway are run through a cord protector, not nailed to the frame.

test.question: A 120/208-volt panel (150 volts or less to ground) has exposed live parts on one side and no live or grounded parts on the other. What is the minimum working clearance in front of it under Table K-1 of 1926.403(i)(1)(i)?
test.explanation: For 0-150 volts to ground, Table K-1 requires 3 feet for conditions (a), (b), and (c). For 151-600 volts, it requires 3, 3.5, or 4 feet depending on the condition. Workspace must also be at least 30 inches wide (1926.403(i)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: keep 3 feet clear in front of the temporary panel; no material staging there.

test.question: Before work begins, what does 1926.416(a)(3) require the employer to determine?
options: Whether any part of an energized electric power circuit, exposed or concealed, is located so the work could bring a person, tool, or machine into contact with it, with warning signs posted and employees advised
Nothing; electricians check as they go
Only the location of the main panel
test.explanation: Before work begins, the employer must find out by inquiry, direct observation, or instruments whether any energized circuit, exposed or concealed, could be contacted during the work. Where one exists, the employer must post and maintain warning signs and advise employees (1926.416(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: before core drilling a wall, check drawings and scan for live conduits.

test.question: Workers will use jackhammers where the exact location of underground power lines is unknown. What does 1926.416(a)(2) require?
options: Insulated protective gloves for employees using jackhammers, bars, or other hand tools that may contact a line
test.explanation: Where the exact location of underground electric powerlines is unknown, employees using jackhammers, bars, or other hand tools that may contact a line must be given insulated protective gloves (1926.416(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew breaking a slab over an unknown duct bank wears rated insulating gloves.

title: Lockout and Tagging of Circuits (Construction)
topics: Rendering deenergized circuits inoperative and tagging every energizing point
Locating energized circuits and posting warnings

resources.title: Lockout and Tagging of Circuits
resources.description: Construction requirements for tagging controls and deenergized circuits

resources.title: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
resources.description: Protection from energized circuits during construction

resources.title: LOTO eTool
resources.description: Interactive LOTO training. The full energy control program (written procedures, periodic inspection, training certification) is covered in the 1910 track, Week 2 (29 CFR 1910.147).

test.question: Under 1926.417(a), what must be done to controls that are to be deactivated while work is done on energized or deenergized equipment or circuits?
options: Nothing if the electrician is nearby
test.explanation: Controls that are to be deactivated during work on energized or deenergized equipment or circuits must be tagged (1926.417(a)). Job-site scenario: the motor starter switched off for conduit work gets a tag before the crew starts. (The full lockout program, including who removes devices, is 1910.147 and is covered in 1910 Week 2.)

test.question: Under 1926.417(b), what is required for equipment or circuits that are deenergized?
options: A sign at the main panel only
A verbal warning to the crew
Nothing if the breaker is off
They must be rendered inoperative and have tags attached at all points where they can be energized
test.explanation: Deenergized equipment or circuits must be rendered inoperative and have tags attached at all points where they can be energized (1926.417(b)). Job-site scenario: a feeder that can be energized from two panels is made inoperative and tagged at both.

test.question: Under 1926.417(c), how must tags be placed?
options: To identify plainly the equipment or circuits being worked on
test.explanation: Tags must be placed to plainly identify the equipment or circuits being worked on (1926.417(c)). Job-site scenario: the tag on breaker 14 reads "Panel LP-2, circuit 14, lighting Level 3 - men working."

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(1), how must an employee be protected before working where they could contact part of an electric power circuit?
options: By trying to operate the equipment
By deenergizing the circuit and grounding it, or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means
test.explanation: An employee may not work where they could contact any part of an electric power circuit unless protected by deenergizing and grounding it, or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means (1926.416(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: after tagging the circuit, the electrician tests it dead and applies grounds before working on the conductors.

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(3), what must the employer do before work begins near possibly energized circuits?
options: Find out by inquiry, observation, or instruments whether energized circuits could be contacted; post and maintain warning signs; and advise employees
test.explanation: The employer must determine whether any part of an energized circuit, exposed or concealed, could be contacted during the work. Where one exists, it must post and maintain warning signs and advise employees of its location and hazards (1926.416(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: before demo of a ceiling, the crew locates live branch circuits and flags them.

test.question: Under 1926.416(d), what must be used to install or remove fuses when one or both terminals are energized?
options: Special tools insulated for the voltage
test.explanation: Fuses installed or removed with one or both terminals energized require special tools insulated for the voltage (1926.416(d)). Job-site scenario: an insulated fuse puller is used on the energized switch.

test.question: Under 1926.416(b)(1), what must be provided when energized parts of electrical equipment are exposed?
options: Barriers or other guarding so the workspace is not used as a passageway
test.explanation: Barriers or other guarding must keep the workspace for electrical equipment from being used as a passageway while energized parts are exposed (1926.416(b)(1)). Working spaces and walkways must be kept clear of cords (1926.416(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: caution tape and stanchions close the corridor in front of the open switchboard.

test.question: In an existing installation, what does 1926.416(c) prohibit?
options: Changing circuit protection to increase the load beyond the load rating of the circuit wiring
test.explanation: In existing installations, no change in circuit protection may be made to increase the load beyond the load rating of the circuit wiring (1926.416(c)). Job-site scenario: a 15-amp breaker on 14-gauge wire is not swapped for a 30-amp to stop nuisance trips.

test.question: A crew finds a frayed extension cord on the job. Under 1926.416(e)(1), what is required?
options: Tape it and keep using it
Worn or frayed cords may not be used
test.explanation: Worn or frayed electric cords or cables may not be used (1926.416(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: the frayed cord is tagged out and removed (see also 1926.20(b)(3)).

test.question: Under 1926.20(b)(3), how may equipment that does not comply with Part 1926 be taken out of use?
options: It may stay in use until the shift ends
By telling the operator not to use it
By tagging it as unsafe or locking its controls so it cannot be operated, or by physically removing it
test.explanation: Noncompliant machinery, tools, materials, or equipment must be identified as unsafe by tagging or locking the controls to make them inoperable, or physically removed (1926.20(b)(3)). This is the general 1926 basis for locking out controls. Job-site scenario: a saw table with a broken guard has its disconnect locked and tagged.

title: Excavation Safety Basics
topics: Sloping in Type C soil and the default slope

test.question: Under 1926.652(a)(1), when is a protective system NOT required in an excavation?
options: When it is made entirely in stable rock, or is less than 5 feet deep and a competent person finds no indication of a potential cave-in
When the excavation is less than 8 feet deep
When work will take less than an hour
test.explanation: Each employee in an excavation must be protected from cave-ins by an adequate protective system, except in excavations made entirely in stable rock, or less than 5 feet deep where a competent person's examination shows no indication of a potential cave-in (1926.652(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a 5.5-foot water-line trench needs a protective system.

test.question: When must a competent person inspect excavations under 1926.651(k)(1)?
options: Daily before work starts, as needed throughout the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence
test.explanation: Daily inspections of excavations, adjacent areas, and protective systems must be made by a competent person before work starts and as needed throughout the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence, when employee exposure can be reasonably anticipated (1926.651(k)(1)). Job-site scenario: after an overnight storm, the competent person inspects before anyone enters.

test.question: What is the maximum allowable slope for a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep in Type C soil (1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, B-1.3)?
test.explanation: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less deep in Type C soil have a maximum allowable slope of 1 1/2:1 (horizontal:vertical) (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.3)). Job-site scenario: an 8-foot-deep cut in sandy Type C soil is laid back 12 feet horizontally on each side.

test.question: If the employer does not classify the soil, what slope does Option (1) of 1926.652(b)(1)(i) require?
options: Vertical sides are fine under 10 feet
No steeper than 1 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical (34 degrees from horizontal)
test.explanation: Under Option (1), excavations must be sloped no steeper than 1 1/2H:1V (34 degrees from horizontal) unless another option is used (1926.652(b)(1)(i)), in Type C configurations (1926.652(b)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: with no competent-person soil classification, the crew slopes at 1 1/2:1.

test.question: Under 1926.651(c)(2), trench excavations 4 feet or more deep must have a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress located so employees need no more than ___ of lateral travel.
test.explanation: A safe means of egress must be in trenches 4 feet or more deep so employees travel no more than 25 feet laterally to reach it (1926.651(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: in a 100-foot trench, ladders are placed so no one is more than 25 feet from one.

test.question: How far from the edge of an excavation must spoil and equipment be kept under 1926.651(j)(2)?
options: At least 2 feet, or use retaining devices (or both)
test.explanation: Employees must be protected from excavated material or equipment falling or rolling into the excavation by keeping it at least 2 feet from the edge, by retaining devices, or both (1926.651(j)(2)). Job-site scenario: the excavator places spoil at least 2 feet back from the trench lip.

test.question: Under 1926.651(g)(1)(i), when must the atmosphere be tested before employees enter an excavation?
options: Only when there is a visible vapor
When the excavation is more than 4 feet deep and an oxygen deficiency (below 19.5%) or hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected
test.explanation: Where oxygen deficiency (below 19.5%) or a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected, such as near landfills or stored hazardous substances, the atmosphere must be tested before employees enter excavations more than 4 feet deep (1926.651(g)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a trench next to an old fuel tank is tested before entry.

test.question: After soil is classified, conditions change after heavy rain. What does Appendix A to Subpart P require (1926 Subpart P Appendix A (c)(5))?
options: A competent person must evaluate the changes and reclassify the deposit as necessary
test.explanation: If the properties, factors, or conditions affecting a classification change in any way, a competent person must evaluate the changes and reclassify the deposit as necessary (1926 Subpart P Appendix A (c)(5)). Job-site scenario: after saturation, the Type B classification is downgraded to Type C and slopes are cut back.

test.question: If water removal equipment is used to control water in an excavation, what does 1926.651(h)(2) require?
options: The equipment and operations must be monitored by a competent person
Workers must wait until it is fully dry
test.explanation: Employees may not work in excavations with accumulated or accumulating water unless adequate precautions are taken (1926.651(h)(1)). If water removal equipment is used, a competent person must monitor it and its operation (1926.651(h)(2)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks the sump pumps throughout the shift.

test.question: What does 1926.651(a) require for surface encumbrances, such as a sidewalk slab next to a planned trench?
options: Those located so as to create a hazard must be removed or supported as necessary to safeguard employees
test.explanation: All surface encumbrances located so as to create a hazard must be removed or supported as necessary to safeguard employees (1926.651(a)). Job-site scenario: the sidewalk panel next to the trench line is saw-cut and removed before digging alongside it.

resources.title: Excavation Inspection Requirement
resources.description: Daily competent-person inspection of excavations and protective systems

test.question: What is the maximum allowable slope for a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep in Type B soil (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.2))?
test.explanation: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less deep in Type B soil have a maximum allowable slope of 1:1 (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.2)). Job-site scenario: a 6-foot cut in Type B silty clay is laid back 6 feet horizontally.

test.question: In Type B soil, an excavation 20 feet or less deep has a vertically sided lower portion. Per 1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.2), how high must the shield or support extend?
options: At least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side
test.explanation: Excavations 20 feet or less deep with vertically sided lower portions must be shielded or supported to at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side, with a maximum allowable slope of 1:1 above (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.2)). Job-site scenario: a trench box in the bottom of a benched cut sticks up 18 inches past the vertical wall.

test.question: In Type A soil, an excavation 8 feet or less deep has an unsupported vertically sided lower portion. What is the maximum height of that vertical side (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.1))?
test.explanation: Type A excavations 8 feet or less deep with unsupported vertically sided lower portions may have a vertical side no higher than 3 1/2 feet (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.1)). Excavations entirely in stable rock need no protective system (1926.652(a)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a 7-foot Type A cut keeps its bottom vertical wall at 3.5 feet or less.

test.question: How often must protective systems be inspected under 1926.651(k)(1)?
options: Daily by a competent person, before work and as needed during the shift, and after hazard-increasing events
test.explanation: Daily inspections of excavations, adjacent areas, and protective systems must be made by a competent person, before work and as needed throughout the shift, and after rainstorms or other hazard-increasing occurrences (1926.651(k)(1)). If failure indications are found, employees must be removed until it is made safe (1926.651(k)(2)). Job-site scenario: hydraulic shores are checked every morning before entry.

test.question: How must support systems be removed under 1926.652(e)(1)(v)?
options: All at once with the excavator
Starting at and progressing from the bottom of the excavation, releasing members slowly to watch for signs of failure
test.explanation: Removal must begin at and progress from the bottom of the excavation, with members released slowly to note any sign of failure or cave-in (1926.652(e)(1)(v)). Backfilling must progress together with removal (1926.652(e)(1)(vi)). Job-site scenario: the bottom hydraulic shore is released first, then backfill is placed before the next shore comes out.

test.question: When a support or shield system comes from the manufacturer's tabulated data, what does 1926.652(c)(2) require?
options: Nothing needs to be on site
Any engineer may verbally approve changes
Only the box serial number is needed

It must follow all manufacturer specifications, recommendations, and limitations; deviation requires the manufacturer's specific written approval; and the data must be in writing at the jobsite during construction
test.explanation: Designs from manufacturer's tabulated data must follow all of the manufacturer's specifications, recommendations, and limitations (1926.652(c)(2)(i)). Deviation requires the manufacturer's specific written approval (1926.652(c)(2)(ii)). The data and any approvals must be in writing at the jobsite during construction (1926.652(c)(2)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the trench box tab data is in the foreman's truck.

test.question: Trench boxes will be stacked. Under 1926.652(c)(2)(ii), when may the crew deviate from the manufacturer's stacking limits?
options: Only after the manufacturer issues specific written approval
Never question it; any stack height works
If the trench is under 10 feet
test.explanation: Deviation from the manufacturer's specifications, recommendations, and limitations is allowed only after the manufacturer issues specific written approval (1926.652(c)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: stacking a third box beyond the tab data requires a written approval letter from the manufacturer.

test.question: Under 1926.652(g)(1)(iii), how must employees be protected when entering or exiting areas protected by shields?
options: They may move quickly between shields
They must be protected from cave-ins when entering or exiting
test.explanation: Employees must be protected from cave-ins when entering or exiting areas protected by shields (1926.652(g)(1)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the ladder is placed inside the trench box so workers never step into the unprotected trench.

test.question: A loader will work next to a trench, and the operator cannot see the edge. What does 1926.651(f) require?
options: A warning system such as barricades, hand or mechanical signals, or stop logs
test.explanation: When mobile equipment operates next to or approaches the edge of an excavation and the operator lacks a clear and direct view of the edge, a warning system such as barricades, hand or mechanical signals, or stop logs must be used (1926.651(f)). Job-site scenario: stop logs keep the loader's wheels back from the trench edge.

test.question: Under 1926.652(g)(1)(iv), when may employees NOT be inside a shield?
options: When the shield is more than 10 feet deep
While the shield is being installed, removed, or moved vertically
test.explanation: Employees may not be in shields while they are being installed, removed, or moved vertically (1926.652(g)(1)(iv)). Excavating up to 2 feet below the bottom of a shield is allowed only if it is designed for the full trench depth and there are no signs of loss of soil (1926.652(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: the pipe crew climbs out before the box is dragged forward.

resources.title: Entry Permit
resources.description: Required contents of a construction confined space entry permit

test.question: Under the definitions in 1926.1202, an oxygen-deficient atmosphere contains less than what percentage of oxygen by volume?
test.explanation: An oxygen-deficient atmosphere contains less than 19.5% oxygen by volume. A hazardous atmosphere includes oxygen below 19.5% or above 23.5% (1926.1202 (definitions)). Job-site scenario: the storm drain reads 19.0% oxygen, so entry cannot proceed until it is ventilated and retested.

test.question: After entry into a permit space is authorized, how must entry conditions be monitored under 1926.1204(e)(1)(ii)?
options: Continuously in the areas where entrants work, except that periodic monitoring may be used for a hazard if continuous monitoring equipment is not commercially available
test.explanation: Once entry is authorized, entry conditions must be monitored continuously where authorized entrants are working. Periodic monitoring is allowed only for a hazard where continuous monitoring equipment is not commercially available (1926.1204(e)(1)(ii), (e)(2)). Job-site scenario: a 4-gas meter stays running with the entrant during welding inside the tank.

test.question: Which characteristic makes a confined space a permit-required confined space under 1926.1202?
options: It contains or may contain a hazardous atmosphere, an engulfment material, an inwardly converging or tapering configuration, or any other recognized serious safety or health hazard
test.explanation: A permit space has one or more of these: contains or may contain a hazardous atmosphere; contains material that could engulf an entrant; has an internal configuration that could trap or asphyxiate an entrant; or contains any other recognized serious safety or health hazard (1926.1202 (definitions)). Job-site scenario: a vault with possible sewer gas is a permit space.

test.question: Under 1926.1209, which is a duty of the attendant?
options: Entering the space to help the entrant
Continuously keeping an accurate count of authorized entrants and remaining outside the permit space until relieved by another attendant
test.explanation: The attendant must continuously keep an accurate count of authorized entrants (1926.1209(c)) and remain outside the permit space during entry operations until relieved by another attendant (1926.1209(d)), among other duties. Job-site scenario: at the manhole, the attendant keeps the entrant log and never climbs in.

test.question: Under 1926.1211(c)(2), what must be available to retrieve personnel from vertical permit spaces more than 5 feet deep?
options: Nothing if a rescue team is on call
test.explanation: The retrieval line must attach to a mechanical device or fixed point outside the space, and a mechanical device must be available to retrieve personnel from vertical permit spaces more than 5 feet deep (1926.1211(c)(2)). Non-entry rescue is required unless retrieval equipment would increase risk or not help (1926.1211(c)). Job-site scenario: a tripod and winch are set over the 12-foot sewer manhole.

test.question: When must the entry supervisor cancel an entry permit under 1926.1205(e)?
options: Only at the end of the shift
When the covered entry operations are completed, or when a condition not allowed under the permit arises (suspend or cancel and fully reassess if the condition is temporary)
Never; permits last the whole project
test.explanation: The entry supervisor must terminate entry and cancel the permit when operations are complete (1926.1205(e)(1)), or when a condition not allowed under the permit arises. A temporary condition that creates no new hazard may lead to suspension and full reassessment instead (1926.1205(e)(2)-(3)). Job-site scenario: the ventilation blower fails, entrants exit, and the permit is suspended until reassessed.

test.question: What does 1926.1207(a) require for confined space training?
options: Training at no cost to each employee whose work is regulated, so they have the understanding, knowledge, and skills needed for their assigned duties
test.explanation: The employer must provide training, at no cost, to each employee whose work is regulated by the standard, giving them the understanding, knowledge, and skills to safely perform their assigned duties (1926.1207(a)). Records must include names, trainers, and dates (1926.1207(d)). Job-site scenario: the tank-cleaning crew is trained on the specific hazards of that tank before entry.

test.question: How does 1926.1203(b)(1) require employers to inform exposed employees of a permit space?
options: Only by a verbal warning at the morning meeting
Only by marking the space on drawings
By posting danger signs or other equally effective means; a sign reading "DANGER--PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER" satisfies it
test.explanation: Employers must inform exposed employees of the existence, location, and danger of each permit space by posting danger signs or other equally effective means. "DANGER--PERMIT-REQUIRED CONFINED SPACE, DO NOT ENTER" or similar language satisfies the sign requirement (1926.1203(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the sign is posted at the vault hatch.

test.question: What communication duty does 1926.1209(e) give the attendant?
options: Communicating with authorized entrants as necessary to assess their status and alert them to evacuate
Only at the start of entry
test.explanation: The attendant must communicate with authorized entrants as necessary to assess their status and to alert them of the need to evacuate (1926.1209(e)). The employer must provide the communications equipment needed (1926.1204(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: radio contact between attendant and entrant in a long tunnel.

test.question: Under the alternate entry procedures, what does 1926.1203(e)(2)(v)(A) require before an employee enters a space ventilated with continuous forced air?
options: The employee may not enter until the forced-air ventilation has eliminated any hazardous atmosphere
Entry may begin while the blower warms up
Ventilation only if the supervisor asks
test.explanation: An employee may not enter until forced-air ventilation has eliminated any hazardous atmosphere (1926.1203(e)(2)(v)(A)). Ventilation must be directed to where employees are and continue until all have left (1926.1203(e)(2)(v)(B)). Job-site scenario: the blower runs, the meter reads clean, then entry begins.

test.question: In what order must atmospheric hazards be tested under 1926.1204(e)(3)?
options: Toxic gases, then oxygen, then combustibles
Combustibles first, then toxics, then oxygen
Oxygen first, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors
test.explanation: Testing must check oxygen first, then combustible gases and vapors, then toxic gases and vapors (1926.1204(e)(3)). Job-site scenario: the meter warm-up and readout follow O2, LEL, then H2S and CO.

resources.title: Engineering Survey Requirement
resources.description: Competent-person engineering survey required before demolition

test.question: What does 1926.850(a) require before employees start demolition?
options: A work plan from the owner
An engineering survey of the structure by a competent person, with written evidence that it was performed
test.explanation: Before demolition starts, a competent person must make an engineering survey of the structure to determine the condition of the framing, floors, and walls and the possibility of unplanned collapse, including adjacent structures where employees may be exposed. The employer must have written evidence of the survey (1926.850(a)). Job-site scenario: the survey of a fire-damaged warehouse is on file before the crew goes in.

test.question: Under 1926.850(c), when must electric, gas, water, steam, sewer, and other service lines be shut off, capped, or controlled?
options: Before demolition work is started, outside the building line, with any involved utility company notified in advance
At the end of the day
test.explanation: All service lines must be shut off, capped, or otherwise controlled outside the building line before demolition starts, and any involved utility company notified in advance (1926.850(c)). Job-site scenario: gas is capped at the meter and electric is disconnected by the utility before demolition begins.

test.question: Under 1926.252(a), material dropped more than how many feet to a point outside the building's exterior walls requires an enclosed chute?
test.explanation: Whenever materials are dropped more than 20 feet to any point outside the exterior walls, an enclosed chute must be used (1926.252(a)). Under 1926.852(a), no material may be dropped outside the exterior walls unless the area is effectively protected. Job-site scenario: debris from the third floor goes down an enclosed chute into the dumpster.

test.question: What does 1926.850(i) require for floor openings not used as material drops?
options: Covering at the end of the shift
Covering with material strong enough to support any load that may be imposed, secured against accidental movement
test.explanation: Floor openings not used as material drops must be covered with material substantial enough to support any load that may be imposed, and secured to prevent accidental movement (1926.850(i)). Job-site scenario: the hole left by a removed floor drain is covered and screwed down.

test.question: Under 1926.859(g), what inspections are required during demolition?
options: Continuing inspections by a competent person as the work progresses, to detect hazards from weakened floors or walls or loosened material
test.explanation: During demolition, a competent person must make continuing inspections as the work progresses to detect hazards from weakened or deteriorated floors or walls or loosened material. No one may work where such hazards exist until they are corrected (1926.859(g)). Job-site scenario: the competent person watches the wall as the excavator pulls each section.

test.question: Under 1926.850(e), what must be done if hazardous chemicals, gases, or flammable materials may have been used in pipes or tanks on the property?
options: Testing and purging must be performed and the hazard eliminated before demolition starts
test.explanation: The employer must determine whether hazardous chemicals, gases, explosives, flammables, or similar substances were used in pipes, tanks, or equipment. If their presence is apparent or suspected, testing and purging must be performed and the hazard eliminated before demolition starts (1926.850(e)). Asbestos has its own standard (1926.1101). Job-site scenario: an old fuel oil tank is purged and tested before it is cut.

test.question: Under 1926.850(j), in what order must exterior walls and floor construction be demolished?
options: Beginning at the top of the structure and proceeding downward
test.explanation: Except for necessary preparatory work, demolition of exterior walls and floor construction must begin at the top and proceed downward, with each story removed before work starts on the one below (1926.850(j)). Job-site scenario: the roof and top floor come off first.

test.question: Debris is dropped through floor holes without chutes. What does 1926.850(h) require for the area where it lands?
options: Nothing if a spotter is present
It must be completely enclosed with barricades at least 42 inches high and at least 6 feet back from the projected edge of the opening above, with warning signs at each level
test.explanation: The drop area must be completely enclosed with barricades at least 42 inches high and at least 6 feet back from the projected edge of the opening above. Signs warning of falling material must be posted at each level, and removal from that area is not allowed until debris handling above stops (1926.850(h)). Job-site scenario: barricades surround the drop zone below the slab openings.

test.question: Under 1926.854(b), may a masonry wall section more than one story high stand alone without lateral bracing?
options: Only if it is under 30 feet
No, unless it was designed to stand without lateral support and is safe enough to be self-supporting; all walls must be left stable at the end of each shift
test.explanation: No wall section more than one story high may stand alone without lateral bracing unless it was designed to stand without it and is in a safe, self-supporting condition. All walls must be left stable at the end of each shift (1926.854(b)). Job-site scenario: a two-story gable wall is braced before the crew leaves for the day.

test.question: Under 1926.850(k), how must employee entrances to a multi-story structure being demolished be protected?
options: By sidewalk sheds or canopies extending at least 8 feet from the building face, at least 2 feet wider than the opening, and able to hold 150 psf
By a hard hat requirement only
test.explanation: Employee entrances must be completely protected by sidewalk sheds or canopies providing protection at least 8 feet from the face of the building, at least 2 feet wider than the entrance, and capable of sustaining 150 pounds per square foot (1926.850(k)). Job-site scenario: a plywood canopy protects the only crew entrance during facade demolition.
